issue: Does a due process violation from the government's selective grant or withholding of immunity require proof that the prosecutor subjectively intended to distort the fact-finding process, or is it enough that the immunity decision in fact distorted fact-finding?
provision: U.S. Const. amend. V (due process); 18 U.S.C. §§ 6002, 6003(b)

sides.position: Due process is violated only if the government immunizes or withholds immunity from witnesses with the intention of distorting the fact-finding process (the Davis standard), with no further requirement of subjective intent.
cases: United States v. Davis, 845 F.3d 282 (7th Cir. 2016)
United States v. Newton, 76 F.4th 662 (7th Cir. 2023)

sides.position: In addition to distorting the fact-finding process, the prosecutor must have subjectively intended to cause that manipulation.
cases: United States v. Newton, 76 F.4th 662 (7th Cir. 2023)

quote: The parties also disagree about which side of a circuit split we have come down on in regard to whether, in addition to distorting the fact-finding process, the prosecutor must have subjectively intended to cause such manipulation.
cite: United States v. Angelita Newton, 76 F.4th 662 (7th Cir. 2023)
